title: What Do You Ship When the Tax Is Bigger Than the Margin?

October 2023, Indian real-money gaming. Three of the things we shipped, we pulled within weeks. Abhishek Anand 7 min read · Sep 24, 2026 -- Listen Share On 1 October 2023 a 28% tax landed on the full value of every deposit made on a real-money gaming platform in India. Not on revenue. On the deposit. We earned somewhere around ₹17 to ₹19 of gross revenue for every ₹100 a user put in. So the tax on a deposit was larger than the money we made from it. I have read that sentence many times since and it has never improved. Several platforms in the category ran the same arithmetic over the following weeks and shut down. The options in the room were the ones you would expect. Charge more. Pass the tax to the user, so ₹100 in becomes ₹78 of usable balance. Or hold back 28% of every deposit as a locked balance against the liability. All three make the spreadsheet work, which is what makes them dangerous, because a spreadsheet that works is very persuasive at eleven at night in a week like that one. Asking why until it got uncomfortable What follows was not a flash of insight and I would rather not have it written up as one. It was asking why a few more times than felt productive, in a room where everyone already wanted to move to solutions. Why are we underwater? Because every deposit is taxed. Why are there so many deposits? Because users withdraw and re-deposit constantly. Why do they do that? Because we had made money withdrawable almost instantly, and so people took their balance out at night and put it back the next morning. The same ₹100 was getting taxed again and again. In Predictor, our peer-to-peer trading product, a user might churn the same money twenty times in an evening. Every one of those round trips through the wallet was a fresh taxable deposit. The rate was fixed by the government. The number of times we paid it was not. That is a much better problem to have, and it took a week of arguing to see it. It also set a constraint that made everything afterwards harder. We could go after the cycling, but not in a way that made a user feel their own money was being held somewhere they could not reach. The two we turned down Locking 28% of every deposit was the cleanest solution available. Book ₹28 of each ₹100 as non-withdrawable, cover the exposure, sleep well. We did not do it. It holds a user’s money against their will and calls it accounting, and the resentment lasts long after the tax stops being news. Full pass-through was the honest one. ₹100 in, ₹78 usable, tax shown plainly. I still think it was the right answer in the abstract. It only works if the whole category moves at once, though, and nobody was going to. A user comparing wallet credit across four apps does not read the fine print explaining why ours is lower. Being the only honest platform is just being the expensive one. These were not my calls alone. They were argued over more times than I can count, and the argument was mostly about how much trust we were willing to spend to make the maths easier. The answer we landed on was none, and that turned out to be the expensive choice in the short term. What we shipped, and what we pulled back The one that carried most of the weight was slow-wagering. Instead of money becoming withdrawable the moment it settled, a share of what a user wagered converted to withdrawable balance gradually. We started at 25% and tuned it down to 5% over weeks of watching complaints and behaviour. Nobody fought us on it, which surprised me. My read is that in a product where you might cycle the same money twenty times in a night, users had a working intuition for what the wallet was doing, and they knew what the tax had done to the industry. Several of them said some version of “fair enough.” Then we shipped a flat 5% charge on withdrawals, and that one went badly within days. The feedback was blunt and it was always the same sentence. This is my money, why am I paying to take it out. They were right. We pulled it. What replaced it was better and we should have started there. RFM-based withdrawal rules, so regulars withdrew free, new users got one free withdrawal and then a fee, capped at three withdrawals a week. The cycling that actually hurt us was concentrated in a specific behaviour by a specific group, and a flat fee had charged our most loyal users for it. Two more did not survive. Bonus locking, which booked ₹22 of every ₹100 as playable but not withdrawable, landed poorly for the same reason the flat fee did. And we raised the marketplace commission on winnings from 10% to 25%, which was a mistake on two counts. Users hated it and a competitor could undercut it in an afternoon. We settled at 15%, with 10% for high-value users, and that held. One lever came from the data rather than from a meeting. Withdrawals spiked at month end and deposits spiked at the start of the next month, which is the same money going out and coming back with a tax event attached. So in the last week of each month we offered a 10% bonus to convert withdrawable balance into deposit balance. It broke the loop without touching anyone who did not want it. Look at which ones survived. Everything we reverted had the same defect. It charged a user for the crime of holding their own money. The number, and why you should be suspicious of it Gross revenue per ₹100 deposited went from around ₹20 to ₹45-plus, and stayed there for close to two years.
